lesson_scope: Special variants in Cambridge P1 integration: improper integrals with infinite limits, definite integrals with variable limits to recover parameters, and double integration to recover curve equations from second derivatives with stationary/gradient boundary conditions.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: basic improper integral of x^-2 with infinite upper limit.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of evaluating an improper integral with an infinite upper bound.

hints: Write the integrand using negative exponents: $\dfrac{1}{x^2} = x^{-2}$.
Find the antiderivative: $\int x^{-2} \, dx = \dfrac{x^{-1}}{-1} = -\dfrac{1}{x}$.
Evaluate the limits: $\lim_{t \to \infty} \left(-\dfrac{1}{t}\right) - \left(-\dfrac{1}{1}\right) = 0 - (-1) = 1$.

walkthrough.text:
Express the improper integral using a limit or standard notation:
$$\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2} \, dx = \lim_{t \to \infty} \int_1^t x^{-2} \, dx$$

Find the antiderivative using the power rule:
$$= \lim_{t \to \infty} \left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_1^t = \lim_{t \to \infty} \left(-\frac{1}{t} - \left(-\frac{1}{1}\right)\right)$$

Evaluate the limit as $t 	o \infty$:
$$= 0 - (-1) = 1$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: improper integral with linear composite denominator (2x+1)^-2.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of integrating a linear composite function over an infinite interval.

hints: Rewrite the integrand with a negative index: $(2x + 1)^{-2}$.
Integrate using the linear chain rule: $\int (2x + 1)^{-2} \, dx = \dfrac{(2x + 1)^{-1}}{-1 \times 2} = -\dfrac{1}{2(2x + 1)}$.
Evaluate at $\infty$ and $0$: $0 - \left(-\dfrac{1}{2(1)}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

walkthrough.text:
Write the integrand in index form:
$$\int_0^\infty (2x + 1)^{-2} \, dx$$

Integrate using the reverse chain rule, dividing by the coefficient of $x$ ($2$):
$$= \left[-\frac{1}{2(2x + 1)}\right]_0^\infty$$

Evaluate the limits:
$$= \lim_{x \to \infty} \left(-\frac{1}{2(2x + 1)}\right) - \left(-\frac{1}{2(2(0) + 1)}\right) = 0 - \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Integrates using linear chain rule to obtain $\left[-\frac{1}{2(2x+1)}\right]_0^\infty$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: definite integral with unknown upper limit solved as a quadratic/monomial equation.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of solving for an unknown integration limit from a given integral value.

hints: Integrate the function $2x$ with respect to $x$: $\int_0^k 2x \, dx = [x^2]_0^k$.
Substitute the limits: $k^2 - 0 = k^2$.
Set the result equal to $9$: $k^2 = 9 \implies k = 3$ (since $k > 0$).

walkthrough.text:
Evaluate the definite integral in terms of $k$:
$$\int_0^k 2x \, dx = \left[x^2\right]_0^k = k^2 - 0^2 = k^2$$

Set the evaluated integral equal to the given value $9$ and solve for $k > 0$:
$$k^2 = 9 \implies k = 3 \quad (\text{since } k > 0)$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: double integration from constant second derivative.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of integrating twice to find a curve equation.

hints: Integrate $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6$ once to find the gradient: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6x + c_1$.
Use $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4$ when $x = 0$ to find $c_1$: $6(0) + c_1 = 4 \implies c_1 = 4$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6x + 4$.
Integrate again: $y = 3x^2 + 4x + c_2$. Use the point $(0, 5)$ to find $c_2 = 5 \implies y = 3x^2 + 4x + 5$.

walkthrough.text:
Integrate the second derivative to find the first derivative:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \int 6 \, dx = 6x + c_1$$

Apply the gradient condition $\frac{dy}{dx} = 4$ when $x = 0$:
$$6(0) + c_1 = 4 \implies c_1 = 4 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = 6x + 4$$

Integrate again to find $y$ and apply the point $(0, 5)$:
$$y = \int (6x + 4) \, dx = 3x^2 + 4x + c_2$$
$$3(0)^2 + 4(0) + c_2 = 5 \implies c_2 = 5 \implies y = 3x^2 + 4x + 5$$

ai_rubric.observable: Integrates twice to $y = 3x^2 + c_1x + c_2$ and uses given initial values.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: double integration from linear second derivative with stationary point condition.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of using a stationary point condition (dy/dx = 0) to find the first constant of integration.

hints: Integrate $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 12x$ to get $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6x^2 + c_1$.
A stationary point at $(1, 4)$ means $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$ when $x = 1$: $6(1)^2 + c_1 = 0 \implies c_1 = -6$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6x^2 - 6$.
Integrate again: $y = 2x^3 - 6x + c_2$. Substitute $(1, 4)$: $2(1) - 6(1) + c_2 = 4 \implies -4 + c_2 = 4 \implies c_2 = 8 \implies y = 2x^3 - 6x + 8$.

walkthrough.text:
Integrate the second derivative:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \int 12x \, dx = 6x^2 + c_1$$

Apply the stationary condition $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ at $x = 1$:
$$6(1)^2 + c_1 = 0 \implies c_1 = -6 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = 6x^2 - 6$$

Integrate to find $y$ and substitute the point $(1, 4)$:
$$y = \int (6x^2 - 6) \, dx = 2x^3 - 6x + c_2$$
$$2(1)^3 - 6(1) + c_2 = 4 \implies -4 + c_2 = 4 \implies c_2 = 8$$
$$y = 2x^3 - 6x + 8$$

ai_rubric.observable: Integrates to $\frac{dy}{dx} = 6x^2 + c_1$, uses $\frac{dy}{dx}(1) = 0$ to find $c_1 = -6$, and integrates again.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: improper integral with fractional negative power x^-3/2.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of integrating a fractional negative power over an infinite domain.

hints: Express the integrand with a fractional exponent: $x^{-3/2}$.
Integrate using the power rule: $\int x^{-3/2} \, dx = \dfrac{x^{-1/2}}{-1/2} = -2x^{-1/2} = -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}}$.
Evaluate at $\infty$ and $1$: $0 - \left(-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{1}}\right) = 0 - (-2) = 2$.

walkthrough.text:
Write the integrand in index notation:
$$\int_1^\infty x^{-3/2} \, dx$$

Apply the power rule to integrate:
$$= \left[\frac{x^{-1/2}}{-1/2}\right]_1^\infty = \left[-2x^{-1/2}\right]_1^\infty = \left[-\frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}\right]_1^\infty$$

Evaluate the limits:
$$= \lim_{x \to \infty} \left(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}\right) - \left(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{1}}\right) = 0 - (-2) = 2$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Easy: improper integral with linear composite reciprocal power.

parts.difficulty_reason: Easy: improper integral with linear composite reciprocal power.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires evaluating an improper integral with an infinite upper limit.

hints: Write the integrand in index form: $6(x + 1)^{-2}$.
Evaluate at upper limit $\infty$ ($\lim_{x \to \infty} -\dfrac{6}{x+1} = 0$) and lower limit $x = 2$ ($-\dfrac{6}{2+1} = -2$).
Subtract to obtain the exact value: $0 - (-2) = 2$.

walkthrough.text:
Write the integrand in index form:
$$\int_2^\infty 6(x + 1)^{-2} \, dx$$

Find the antiderivative using the linear reverse chain rule:
$$= \left[-6(x + 1)^{-1}\right]_2^\infty = \left[-\frac{6}{x + 1}\right]_2^\infty$$

Evaluate the difference as $x 	o \infty$ and at $x = 2$:
$$= \lim_{x \to \infty} \left(-\frac{6}{x + 1}\right) - \left(-\frac{6}{2 + 1}\right) = 0 - (-2) = 2$$

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the upper-limit value $0$ and the lower-limit value $-2$.
Subtracts the limit values to obtain $2$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Easy: integrate twice from constant second derivative and use stationary point to determine both constants.

parts.difficulty_reason: Easy: integrate twice from constant second derivative and use stationary point to determine both constants.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires double integration from d^2y/dx^2 and stationary point conditions.

hints: Integrate $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 4$ to obtain $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4x + c_1$.
At a stationary point $(1, 3)$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$ when $x = 1$: $4(1) + c_1 = 0 \implies c_1 = -4$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4x - 4$.
Integrate again: $y = 2x^2 - 4x + c_2$.
Substitute the point $(1, 3)$ into the equation: $3 = 2(1)^2 - 4(1) + c_2 \implies 3 = -2 + c_2 \implies c_2 = 5$, giving $y = 2x^2 - 4x + 5$.

walkthrough.text:
Integrate the second derivative once:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \int 4 \, dx = 4x + c_1$$

Use the stationary point condition $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ at $x = 1$ to find $c_1$:
$$4(1) + c_1 = 0 \implies c_1 = -4 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = 4x - 4$$

Integrate a second time to find $y$:
$$y = \int (4x - 4) \, dx = 2x^2 - 4x + c_2$$

Use the point $(1, 3)$ to determine $c_2$:
$$3 = 2(1)^2 - 4(1) + c_2 \implies 3 = -2 + c_2 \implies c_2 = 5$$
$$\text{Equation of the curve: } y = 2x^2 - 4x + 5$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: improper integral with linear composite fractional negative power (2x-1)^(-3/2).

parts.difficulty_reason: Medium: improper integral with linear composite fractional negative power (2x-1)^(-3/2).

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires integrating a fractional composite power over an infinite domain.

hints: Write the integrand in index form: $8(2x - 1)^{-3/2}$.
Integrate using the linear chain rule: $\int 8(2x - 1)^{-3/2} \, dx = 8 \cdot \dfrac{(2x - 1)^{-1/2}}{-1/2 \times 2} = -\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{2x - 1}}$.
Evaluate at upper limit $\infty$: $\lim_{x \to \infty} -\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{2x - 1}} = 0$.
Evaluate at lower limit $x = 3$: $-\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{2(3) - 1}} = -\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{5}}$, then subtract: $0 - \left(-\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{5}}\right) = \dfrac{8}{\sqrt{5}}$.

walkthrough.text:
Rewrite the integrand in index form:
$$\int_3^\infty 8(2x - 1)^{-3/2} \, dx$$

Integrate using the reverse chain rule (dividing by the inner derivative $2$):
$$= \left[\frac{8(2x - 1)^{-1/2}}{(-1/2)(2)}\right]_3^\infty = \left[-8(2x - 1)^{-1/2}\right]_3^\infty = \left[-\frac{8}{\sqrt{2x - 1}}\right]_3^\infty$$

Evaluate at the upper limit ($x 	o \infty$) and lower limit ($x = 3$):
$$= \lim_{x \to \infty} \left(-\frac{8}{\sqrt{2x - 1}}\right) - \left(-\frac{8}{\sqrt{2(3) - 1}}\right) = 0 - \left(-\frac{8}{\sqrt{5}}\right) = \frac{8}{\sqrt{5}} \quad \left(\text{or } \frac{8\sqrt{5}}{5}\right)$$

ai_rubric.observable: Integrates with the inner factor to obtain $-8(2x - 1)^{-1/2}$.
Uses the upper-limit value $0$ and lower-limit value $-8/\sqrt{5}$.
Obtains $8/\sqrt{5}$ in an exact equivalent form.

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: integrate with variable upper limit k, set equal to 15, and solve a quadratic equation with surd roots.

parts.difficulty_reason: Medium: integrate with variable upper limit k, set equal to 15, and solve a quadratic equation with surd roots.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires setting up a definite integral in terms of an unknown limit and solving the resulting quadratic.

hints: Integrate the linear polynomial: $\int_1^k (4x - 2) \, dx = \left[2x^2 - 2x\right]_1^k$.
Substitute the limits: $(2k^2 - 2k) - (2(1)^2 - 2(1)) = 2k^2 - 2k$.
Set equal to $15$: $2k^2 - 2k = 15 \implies 2k^2 - 2k - 15 = 0$.
Apply the quadratic formula: $k = \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 4(2)(-15)}}{4} = \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{124}}{4} = \dfrac{1 \pm \sqrt{31}}{2}$. Since $k > 1$, retain $k = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{31}}{2}$.

walkthrough.text:
Evaluate the definite integral in terms of $k$:
$$\int_1^k (4x - 2) \, dx = \left[2x^2 - 2x\right]_1^k = (2k^2 - 2k) - (2(1)^2 - 2(1)) = 2k^2 - 2k$$

Set the expression equal to $15$ and form a quadratic equation:
$$2k^2 - 2k = 15 \implies 2k^2 - 2k - 15 = 0$$

Solve using the quadratic formula:
$$k = \frac{-(-2) \pm \sqrt{(-2)^2 - 4(2)(-15)}}{2(2)} = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 120}}{4} = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{124}}{4} = \frac{2 \pm 2\sqrt{31}}{4} = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{31}}{2}$$

Apply the condition $k > 1$:
$$\text{Since } \sqrt{31} \approx 5.57, \quad \frac{1 + \sqrt{31}}{2} \approx 3.28 > 1 \implies k = \frac{1 + \sqrt{31}}{2}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the quadratic formula to obtain $k = (1 \pm \sqrt{31})/2$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: double integration from linear d^2y/dx^2 = 6x + 4 with given gradient at origin and point (-1, 2).

parts.difficulty_reason: Medium: double integration from linear d^2y/dx^2 = 6x + 4 with given gradient at origin and point (-1, 2).

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires double integration from a linear second derivative with boundary conditions on gradient and coordinate point.

hints: Integrate $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6x + 4$ once: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 + 4x + c_1$.
Use the gradient condition $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1$ when $x = 0$: $3(0)^2 + 4(0) + c_1 = 1 \implies c_1 = 1$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 + 4x + 1$.
Integrate again to find $y$: $y = x^3 + 2x^2 + x + c_2$.

walkthrough.text:
Integrate the second derivative to find the gradient function:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \int (6x + 4) \, dx = 3x^2 + 4x + c_1$$

Apply the condition $\frac{dy}{dx} = 1$ at $x = 0$:
$$3(0)^2 + 4(0) + c_1 = 1 \implies c_1 = 1 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 + 4x + 1$$

Integrate a second time to find the curve equation:
$$y = \int (3x^2 + 4x + 1) \, dx = x^3 + 2x^2 + x + c_2$$

Substitute the point $(-1, 2)$ to find $c_2$:
$$2 = (-1)^3 + 2(-1)^2 + (-1) + c_2 \implies 2 = -1 + 2 - 1 + c_2 \implies c_2 = 2$$
$$\text{Equation of the curve: } y = x^3 + 2x^2 + x + 2$$

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the gradient condition at $x = 0$ to form $1 = c_1$.
Obtains $c_1 = 1$ and states the complete first derivative.
Integrates again to obtain $y = x^3 + 2x^2 + x + c_2$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Hard: evaluate an integral with algebraic limits k^2 and 4k^2 involving both positive and negative fractional powers, simplify to a quadratic in k, and solve for k > 0.

parts.difficulty_reason: Hard: evaluate an integral with algebraic limits k^2 and 4k^2 involving both positive and negative fractional powers, simplify to a quadratic in k, and solve for k > 0.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires evaluating an integral with parameter-dependent limits and solving for the positive parameter.

hints: Write the integrand using fractional powers: $\dfrac{1}{k}x^{1/2} + x^{-1/2}$.
Integrate: $\left[\dfrac{2}{3k}x^{3/2} + 2x^{1/2}\right]_{k^2}^{4k^2}$.
Evaluate at upper limit $4k^2$: $\dfrac{2}{3k}(8k^3) + 2(2k) = \dfrac{16}{3}k^2 + 4k$. At lower limit $k^2$: $\dfrac{2}{3k}(k^3) + 2(k) = \dfrac{2}{3}k^2 + 2k$. Difference: $\dfrac{14}{3}k^2 + 2k$.
Set equal to $\dfrac{68}{3}$: $\dfrac{14}{3}k^2 + 2k = \dfrac{68}{3} \implies 14k^2 + 6k - 68 = 0 \implies 7k^2 + 3k - 34 = 0 \implies (7k + 17)(k - 2) = 0 \implies k = 2$.

walkthrough.text:
Write the integrand in index form and find the antiderivative:
$$\int \left(\frac{1}{k}x^{1/2} + x^{-1/2}\right) \, dx = \left[\frac{2x^{3/2}}{3k} + 2x^{1/2}\right]_{k^2}^{4k^2}$$

Evaluate at the upper limit $x = 4k^2$ and lower limit $x = k^2$ (since $k > 0$, $\sqrt{4k^2} = 2k$ and $(4k^2)^{3/2} = 8k^3$):
$$\text{At } x = 4k^2: \quad \frac{2(8k^3)}{3k} + 2(2k) = \frac{16}{3}k^2 + 4k$$
$$\text{At } x = k^2: \quad \frac{2(k^3)}{3k} + 2(k) = \frac{2}{3}k^2 + 2k$$
$$\text{Difference} = \left(\frac{16}{3} - \frac{2}{3}\right)k^2 + (4 - 2)k = \frac{14}{3}k^2 + 2k$$

Equate to $\frac{68}{3}$ and form a quadratic equation:
$$\frac{14}{3}k^2 + 2k = \frac{68}{3} \implies 14k^2 + 6k - 68 = 0 \implies 7k^2 + 3k - 34 = 0$$

Factor the quadratic and solve for $k > 0$:
$$(7k + 17)(k - 2) = 0 \implies k = -\frac{17}{7} \quad \text{or} \quad k = 2$$
Since $k > 0$, we have $k = 2$.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses $k > 0$ while applying the limits to obtain $\dfrac{14}{3}k^2 + 2k$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Hard: two-part question requiring double integration from a quadratic second derivative d^2y/dx^2 = 12x^2 - 4 to find a quartic curve, then finding all other stationary points by solving a cubic derivative equation.

parts.label: (a)

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires double integration from a quadratic second derivative.

hints: Integrate $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 12x^2 - 4$ once: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4x^3 - 4x + c_1$.
Since $(1, 3)$ is a stationary point, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$ at $x = 1$: $4(1)^3 - 4(1) + c_1 = 0 \implies c_1 = 0$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4x^3 - 4x$.
Integrate again to find $y$: $y = x^4 - 2x^2 + c_2$.
Substitute $(1, 3)$ into the curve equation: $3 = 1^4 - 2(1)^2 + c_2 \implies 3 = -1 + c_2 \implies c_2 = 4$, giving $y = x^4 - 2x^2 + 4$.

walkthrough.text:
Integrate the second derivative once:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \int (12x^2 - 4) \, dx = 4x^3 - 4x + c_1$$

Use the stationary point condition $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ at $x = 1$ to find $c_1$:
$$4(1)^3 - 4(1) + c_1 = 0 \implies c_1 = 0 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = 4x^3 - 4x$$

Integrate a second time to find $y$:
$$y = \int (4x^3 - 4x) \, dx = x^4 - 2x^2 + c_2$$

Use the point $(1, 3)$ to determine $c_2$:
$$3 = 1^4 - 2(1)^2 + c_2 \implies 3 = -1 + c_2 \implies c_2 = 4$$
$$\text{Equation of the curve: } y = x^4 - 2x^2 + 4$$

ai_rubric.observable: Integrates again to obtain $y = x^4 - 2x^2 + c_2$.

parts.label: (b)

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Requires finding all remaining stationary points of the recovered curve.

hints: Set the first derivative equal to zero: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4x^3 - 4x = 0$.
Factor completely: $4x(x^2 - 1) = 4x(x - 1)(x + 1) = 0 \implies x = 0, x = 1, x = -1$.
The given stationary point is at $x = 1$. The other two stationary points are at $x = 0$ and $x = -1$.

walkthrough.text:
Set the first derivative $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ to find stationary points:
$$4x^3 - 4x = 0$$

Factor the cubic expression:
$$4x(x^2 - 1) = 0 \implies 4x(x - 1)(x + 1) = 0$$
$$x = 0, \quad x = 1, \quad x = -1$$

Identify the other $x$-coordinates ($x = 0$ and $x = -1$) and find their corresponding $y$-coordinates on $y = x^4 - 2x^2 + 4$:
$$\text{At } x = 0: \quad y = 0^4 - 2(0)^2 + 4 = 4 \implies (0, 4)$$
$$\text{At } x = -1: \quad y = (-1)^4 - 2(-1)^2 + 4 = 1 - 2 + 4 = 3 \implies (-1, 3)$$
$$\text{Other stationary points: } (0, 4) \text{ and } (-1, 3)$$

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies the other stationary $x$-coordinates as $-1$ and $0$.
Substitutes in the curve equation to obtain $(-1, 3)$ and $(0, 4)$.
